lessonTitle: Inflammatory Skin Disease: Eczema, Psoriasis, Acne and the Language of the Rash

blocks.text: A 19-year-old student develops red, well-demarcated, thickly scaled patches on both elbows and knees two weeks after a sore throat. When he scratches a new insect bite on his forearm, a line of the same scaly rash appears along the scratch a few days later. Dermatologists describe skin in a precise vocabulary, because the shape, surface and distribution of a lesion often give the diagnosis before any test.

blocks.markdown:
### Describing skin lesions

A clear description uses standard terms for **primary lesions** (the basic change) and **secondary changes** (those that follow scratching, healing or time). A **macule** is a flat, circumscribed change in colour less than 1 cm; a **patch** is the same but 1 cm or larger. A **papule** is a raised solid lesion less than 1 cm; a **plaque** is a raised, flat-topped lesion 1 cm or larger; a **nodule** is a solid, deeper lesion 1 cm or larger. A **vesicle** is a fluid-filled blister less than 1 cm; a **bulla** is a fluid-filled blister of 1 cm or more; a **pustule** contains pus. Secondary changes include **scale** (flaking stratum corneum), **excoriation** (scratch marks), **crust** and **lichenification** (thickened skin with accentuated markings from chronic rubbing).

rows: Flat colour change, 1 cm or more
Raised flat-topped lesion, 1 cm or more
Deep solid lesion, 1 cm or more

blocks.markdown:
### Eczema

**Eczema (dermatitis)** is a pruritic inflammatory skin condition. **Atopic eczema** is the commonest form, with a personal or family history of atopy (asthma, hay fever). A defective skin barrier, often from loss-of-function mutations in **filaggrin**, allows water loss and allergen entry, and a Th2-weighted immune response drives itch and inflammation. **Acute** eczema shows erythema, vesicles and weeping; **chronic** eczema shows dry, scaly, lichenified plaques with excoriations. The distribution changes with age: in infants on the face and extensor surfaces, and in older children and adults on the **flexures** (antecubital and popliteal fossae, neck, wrists). **Itch is the cardinal symptom**.

### Psoriasis

**Psoriasis** is an immune-mediated disease of the skin in which a Th17 response, driven by IL-23 and IL-17, causes rapid keratinocyte proliferation (epidermal turnover of days rather than weeks), with retained nuclei in the stratum corneum (parakeratosis) and epidermal thickening (acanthosis). The classic **chronic plaque** form shows **well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with silvery-white scale** on the **extensor surfaces** (elbows, knees), the scalp and the lumbosacral region. Pinpoint bleeding on removal of scale (**Auspitz sign**), the **Koebner phenomenon** (new lesions at sites of trauma), and nail pitting or onycholysis are characteristic. Triggers include streptococcal infection (guttate form), drugs and stress, and some patients develop psoriatic arthritis.

rows: Ill-defined erythema, vesicles (acute), dry lichenified plaques (chronic)
Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale
Flexures in older children and adults; face and extensors in infants
Extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), scalp, lumbosacral region
Nail pitting, Koebner phenomenon, arthritis, Th17 response
Acanthosis, parakeratosis, neutrophils in the stratum corneum

blocks.title: Describing and diagnosing a rash
blocks.prompt: A 6-year-old has intensely itchy, dry, red scaly patches with scratch marks in the antecubital and popliteal fossae. She has asthma. Describe the lesions and name the condition.

steps.text: The lesions are ill-defined erythematous patches and plaques with scale, with linear excoriations from scratching.
The distribution, in the flexures, is typical for atopic eczema in childhood.
Intense itch and a personal history of atopy (asthma) strengthen the diagnosis. Psoriasis would show well-demarcated silvery plaques on extensors.

blocks.answer: Atopic eczema, with flexural erythematous scaly plaques and excoriation.

blocks.markdown:
### Acne vulgaris and topical treatment

**Acne** is a disease of the pilosebaceous unit in adolescence: androgen-driven sebum production, follicular hyperkeratinisation that blocks the follicle, colonisation by *Cutibacterium acnes* and inflammation. Lesions are **comedones** (open, blackheads; and closed, whiteheads), **papules, pustules**, and in severe disease **nodules** and scarring, over the face, chest and back. Treatment is matched to the pathology.

rows: Restore the skin barrier and reduce water loss
Topical corticosteroids (potency matched to site and severity)
Topical corticosteroids, vitamin D analogues (calcipotriol), coal tar
Topical retinoids (adapalene), benzoyl peroxide, topical antibiotics (with benzoyl peroxide)
blocks.caption: Matching topical treatments to conditions (names are teaching examples, not advice)
A practical rule for estimating the extent of a skin condition using the patient's own hand.

blocks.title: Estimating extent and topical quantity
blocks.prompt: A patient's psoriasis covers an area equal to about 10 of their own palms. One fingertip unit (FTU, about 0.5 g of cream) covers an area about twice the size of the flat adult palm and fingers. Estimate the body surface area involved and the number of FTUs to treat it once (a teaching example, not a dosing instruction).

steps.text: Each palm is about 1% of body surface area, so 10 palms is about 10%.
One FTU covers two palms (about 2%), so 10% needs 10 / 2 = 5 FTUs.
5 FTUs is about 5 x 0.5 g = 2.5 g for a single application, illustrating how quantity scales with area.

blocks.answer: About 10% of body surface area, requiring about 5 FTUs (about 2.5 g) per application.

points: Lesions are described by standard terms: macule and patch are flat, papule and plaque are raised, nodule is deep, and vesicle and bulla are fluid-filled, with scale, excoriation and lichenification as secondary changes.

Atopic eczema is an itchy, barrier-deficient, Th2-driven flexural dermatitis, whereas psoriasis is a Th17-driven disease of well-demarcated silvery-scaled plaques on extensor surfaces with Koebner phenomenon and nail changes.
Topical treatment is matched to mechanism: emollients and steroids for eczema, steroids and vitamin D analogues for psoriasis, and retinoids with benzoyl peroxide for acne.

questions.stem: A dermatologist describes a raised, flat-topped, scaly lesion measuring 3 cm. Which term is correct?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a raised flat-topped lesion of 1 cm or more is a plaque.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: a papule is raised but under 1 cm.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: a macule is flat, not raised.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: a vesicle is fluid-filled and under 1 cm.

questions.explanation: Size and elevation separate the terms: lesions under 1 cm are macules (flat) or papules (raised), and those of 1 cm or more are patches (flat) or plaques (raised). This lesion is raised and 3 cm, so it is a plaque.

questions.stem: Which term describes a fluid-filled blister measuring 5 mm?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: fluid-filled lesions under 1 cm are vesicles.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: a bulla is 1 cm or more.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: a pustule contains pus, not clear fluid.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: a nodule is a deep solid lesion.

questions.explanation: Vesicles and bullae are both fluid-filled, and size distinguishes them: under 1 cm is a vesicle and 1 cm or more is a bulla.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on his knees and elbows, pitting of the nails, and pinpoint bleeding when scale is removed. Which diagnosis is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: silvery-scaled plaques on extensors, nail pitting and the Auspitz sign are characteristic of psoriasis.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: atopic eczema is itchy, ill-defined and flexural.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: acne affects pilosebaceous follicles on face, chest and back.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: irritant dermatitis would be localised to the area of contact and not show nail pitting.

questions.explanation: Rapid keratinocyte turnover produces thick silvery scale on extensor surfaces. Nail pitting and the Auspitz sign are supporting features.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old with asthma has an itchy rash of dry scaly erythematous patches behind both knees and in the elbow creases. Which mechanism is most relevant?

options.text: Skin barrier defect (for example filaggrin loss) with Th2-driven inflammation
Androgen-driven sebum excess with blocked follicles
Fungal invasion of the stratum corneum

questions.correctOptionText: Skin barrier defect (for example filaggrin loss) with Th2-driven inflammation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: atopic eczema involves barrier failure and Th2 responses.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: Th17-driven hyperproliferation is the mechanism of psoriasis.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this is the mechanism of acne.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: fungal infection is not suggested.

questions.explanation: Flexural itchy dermatitis in a child with atopy is atopic eczema. A defective barrier allows irritants and allergens in, and a Th2-weighted response drives itch and inflammation.

questions.stem: Which topical treatment is correctly matched to its main mechanism?

options.text: Adapalene for acne: topical retinoid that normalises follicular keratinisation
Calcipotriol for acne: reduces sebum production
Emollient for acne: kills Cutibacterium acnes
Benzoyl peroxide for psoriasis: inhibits keratinocyte proliferation

questions.correctOptionText: Adapalene for acne: topical retinoid that normalises follicular keratinisation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: retinoids reduce follicular hyperkeratinisation and comedone formation.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: calcipotriol is a vitamin D analogue used in psoriasis.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: emollients restore the barrier and are not antibacterial.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: benzoyl peroxide is antibacterial and used in acne.

questions.explanation: Topical retinoids correct abnormal follicular keratinisation, which is one of the primary events in acne. The other pairings mix up conditions and mechanisms.

questions.stem: A patient's eczema covers an area equal to 12 of their own palms (including fingers). Using the rule that one palm is about 1% of body surface area, estimate the percentage of body surface area involved.
questions.explanation: One palm is approximately 1% of the body surface area, so 12 palms is about 12%. This simple estimate helps to grade severity and to plan the quantity of topical treatment.

questions.stem: As a pharmacology teaching example, one fingertip unit (about 0.5 g of cream) covers about 2% of body surface area. How many grams of cream are needed to cover 14% body surface area once?
questions.explanation: 14% / 2% = 7 fingertip units, and 7 x 0.5 g = 3.5 g. This illustrates why large body areas need much larger quantities of topical steroid, with more potential for absorption and side effects.

questions.stem: Describe the distribution and morphology of atopic eczema and plaque psoriasis, and state one pathogenic mechanism for each.
markingGuide: Eczema: itchy, ill-defined erythema, vesicles and weeping when acute, dry lichenified plaques with excoriation when chronic
Eczema distribution: flexures in older children and adults; face and extensors in infants
Eczema mechanism: filaggrin and barrier defect with Th2-driven inflammation, atopy
Psoriasis: well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale
Psoriasis distribution: extensor surfaces, scalp, lumbosacral; nail pitting, Koebner phenomenon
Psoriasis mechanism: Th17/IL-23 axis with rapid keratinocyte proliferation
questions.explanation: The two conditions differ in surface, border definition, symptom and site because their mechanisms differ: barrier failure with Th2 inflammation in eczema, and hyperproliferation driven by Th17 cytokines in psoriasis.

questions.stem: Define macule, patch, papule, plaque, nodule, vesicle and bulla. Then describe the clinical lesions of acne vulgaris using these terms and explain the pathogenesis.
markingGuide: Macule flat under 1 cm; patch flat 1 cm or more
Papule raised under 1 cm; plaque raised 1 cm or more; nodule deep solid 1 cm or more
Vesicle fluid-filled under 1 cm; bulla 1 cm or more
Acne lesions: comedones (open and closed), papules, pustules, nodules, scarring
Pathogenesis: androgen-driven sebum, follicular hyperkeratinisation, C. acnes colonisation, inflammation
questions.explanation: Size, elevation and contents form a universal grammar for describing skin. Acne lesions map onto these terms and reflect the stage of follicular blockage and inflammation.

questions.stem: Match topical treatments to eczema, psoriasis and acne, giving a mechanism for each treatment named, and explain why emollients are the foundation of eczema care.
markingGuide: Eczema: emollients restore barrier and reduce water loss
Eczema flares: topical corticosteroids (anti-inflammatory); calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus inhibit T-cell activation
Psoriasis: corticosteroids, vitamin D analogues (calcipotriol), coal tar reduce inflammation and proliferation
Acne: topical retinoids normalise keratinisation, benzoyl peroxide is antibacterial, topical antibiotics reduce C. acnes and inflammation
Emollients address the primary barrier defect and reduce flares and steroid need
questions.explanation: Topical therapy targets the dominant pathology of each disease: barrier dysfunction and inflammation in eczema, hyperproliferation and inflammation in psoriasis, and follicular blockage with bacteria in acne.
